title: Four proposed debates to the Backbench Business Committee (3 Nov 2026)
label: 3 November 2026 · Backbench Business Committee applications
summary: Four MPs asked the Committee to allocate debates: Mike Reader on children's safety in online gaming (prefers DCMS; wants an early debate to influence rules); Jim Shannon on ending unhealthy homes and buildings (prefers Thursday and MHCLG involvement); Nesil Caliskan on a Chamber debate for Islamophobia Awareness Month (needs more Opposition signatories, accepts Westminster Hall); and Samantha Niblett on disabled children's social care (uncertain whether DHSC or DfE should respond). The Committee reminded applicants about departmental responsibility, timing, and the need for balanced cross-party lists for Chamber debates; Clerks will follow up.

glossary.definition: A secondary debating chamber in Parliament used for 90‑minute debates, usually with fewer formalities than the main Chamber.

chapters.title: Children's safety on online gaming platforms
chapters.takeaway: Mike Reader asked for an early Westminster Hall debate with DCMS to press for stronger protections for children in online games, especially around voice chat and off‑platform contact.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: First application: a 90-minute Westminster Hall debate from Mike Reader on children's safety on online gaming platforms. Mike, please introduce it.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: Platforms like Roblox are hugely popular with children. Government research shows 40% of offenders first try to contact children online, often via games.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: Gaming is different from social media: there is voice chat, in-game money, user-created worlds and many ways to move a child into private messages off the platform.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: The Government is introducing protections for major platforms, but I want a debate to press DCMS on the scope of rules, age checks and the off‑platform problem before regulations are finalised.

turns.speaker: Will Stone
turns.text: Which Department do you want to respond—DCMS or DfE?

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: DCMS is the right responder because it's leading on online protections and the forthcoming legislation.

turns.speaker: Will Stone
turns.text: Any idea when the Government's overall response to the Growing up in the online world consultation will be published?

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: There have been platform-specific responses, but no comprehensive timetable. I'd like the debate before Christmas or early in the new year.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Clerks will follow up. We can only allocate a Tuesday morning Westminster Hall slot when the answering Department matches that day's rota.

chapters.title: Ending the unhealthy homes and buildings crisis
chapters.takeaway: Jim Shannon seeks a Westminster Hall debate (prefers Thursday) to push for a preventative, cross‑departmental approach to housing that protects health without heavy new regulation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Next, Jim Shannon wants a Westminster Hall debate on ending the unhealthy homes and buildings crisis. Jim, you have the floor.

turns.speaker: Jim Shannon
turns.text: Our homes and buildings can make people sick. With the Government planning 1.5 million homes, we have a once-in-a-generation chance to make health and wellbeing central to housing, energy and planning decisions.

turns.speaker: Jim Shannon
turns.text: I argue for prevention rather than reacting to poor conditions. This won't need burdensome new rules but better alignment across departments and shared outcomes.

turns.speaker: Mary Glindon
turns.text: Are you asking for a Tuesday or Thursday slot?

turns.speaker: Jim Shannon
turns.text: I'm flexible but prefer Thursday; it suits me better for travel.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Which Department would you like to respond—MHCLG (housing) or another Department?

turns.speaker: Jim Shannon
turns.text: I thought MHCLG would be appropriate, but I'm guided by the Committee and happy to be flexible.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: A practical point: you have many names of supporters. If they all spoke in a Westminster Hall debate, each would get only about a minute—attendance often falls short of the number who sign an application.

turns.speaker: Jim Shannon
turns.text: I appreciate that—many people offer support in principle but won't all attend. I'll leave the list with the Clerks and understand the reality.

chapters.title: Debate for Islamophobia Awareness Month
chapters.takeaway: Nesil Caliskan asked for a Chamber debate in November to mark Islamophobia Awareness Month but was told she needs more Opposition signatories; she accepts Westminster Hall if needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Next is Nesil Caliskan, seeking a Chamber debate on Islamophobia Awareness Month. Nesil, explain why this matters now.

turns.speaker: Nesil Caliskan
turns.text: The debate would look at the prevalence and impact of anti‑Muslim hatred, contributions of British Muslims and how to tackle discrimination. November is the natural time because of the awareness month.

turns.speaker: Nesil Caliskan
turns.text: I have cross-party support listed and expect a balanced, well-attended debate, but timing is important to maximise public engagement.

turns.speaker: Martin Vickers
turns.text: November Chamber slots are limited. Would you accept a Westminster Hall debate instead?

turns.speaker: Nesil Caliskan
turns.text: Westminster Hall would be fine, though I prefer November for visibility. December would still be relevant if November is not possible.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: For a Chamber debate we need a balance of Government and Opposition names. Your list is acceptable for Westminster Hall, but to be considered for the Chamber you should add four or five additional Opposition names quickly.

turns.speaker: Nesil Caliskan
turns.text: The omission of some Opposition names was due to time. I can add them and will contact the Clerks promptly.

chapters.title: Disabled children's social care
chapters.takeaway: Samantha Niblett requested a Westminster Hall debate to press for action on disabled children's social care; she asked whether DHSC or DfE should respond and wanted scrutiny of Law Commission recommendations.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Finally, Samantha Niblett wants a Westminster Hall debate on disabled children's social care. Samantha, tell us the problem and what you want from Parliament.

turns.speaker: Samantha Niblett
turns.text: Families depend on respite, personal care, specialist equipment and adaptations, but support is patchy. Workforce shortages and differing local thresholds mean help can simply not arrive.

turns.speaker: Samantha Niblett
turns.text: The Law Commission has proposed a fairer legal framework and SEND reform is on the agenda. A Westminster Hall debate would let MPs share experiences and press for a clear timetable for reform.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: Your application names DHSC as the answering Department, but many responsibilities sit with the DfE. Which do you definitely want to respond?

turns.speaker: Samantha Niblett
turns.text: It's a tough call. This is about social care for disabled children, so either DHSC or DfE could respond. In practice it's about securing better local services—I'm particularly thinking of a child in my constituency who isn't getting support.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Understood. The Clerks will be in touch to sort timing and which Department should answer.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That concludes the public business. We'll retire to consider the applications and the allocation of time; Clerks will contact applicants about dates, required additional names for Chamber debates and departmental answers.
